# Using ISLA {#sec-using}

**ISLA ships as one class with one recommended configuration, trained and
evaluated by the unified external-aerodynamics recipe; this chapter is the
operating manual.** It tells you which configuration to run and why, what
the model needs from your data, the two commands that train and evaluate
it, the learning-rate rule that lets it scale in width, the inference
sampler that removes most of the draw noise at a fixed cell budget, and
what a step costs. Everything here is about ISLA
unless a variant is named; the reasons behind each recommendation are in
@sec-mt2 and the evidence chapters, cited at the point where they apply.

## Which configuration {#sec-using-config}

Use **ISLA as shipped**: the relative frame with the total-measure
length unit. It is the class default, so `ISLA()` with no
frame arguments is it, and the recipe's `isla_surface.yaml` states the two
settings explicitly:

```yaml
model:
  _target_: physicsnemo.experimental.nn.ISLA
  out_scalars: 1        # pressure
  out_vectors: 1        # wall shear stress
  hidden: 192
  n_layers: 12
  n_slices: 256
  mlp_ratio: 4
  frame_mode: relative        # positions enter only as point-to-anchor differences
  scale_mode: total_measure   # length unit = sqrt(total quadrature measure)
  geo_checkpoint: true        # rebuild per-slice geometry in backward: same numbers, half the memory
```

The configuration table below is the whole decision. The similarity-gauge
variant exists because the program measured it; it is not recommended for
new work (@sec-mt2-variants states the open question about it).

| configuration | recipe config | when to use | what you give up |
|---|---|---|---|
| **reference** (relative frame, total-measure scale) | `isla_surface`, `isla_volume` | every new surface or interior task | nothing among ISLA's options; against the baselines, in-distribution accuracy on every surface rung measured, from 2% at the scale corner to 28% at 35 wing cases (@sec-scoreboard) |
| similarity-gauge variant (measure-weighted center and RMS radius) | `similarity_gauge: true` on a centered frame | a diagnostic comparison of frame choices | a frame still estimated from the sample; equal accuracy to the reference |
| passive decoder (`query_independent: true`) | `isla_volume_support` | when the prediction at a point must not depend on which other points are queried | 3.0 to 3.7x in accuracy (@sec-query-independence) |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The legacy centered variant (diagnostic)"}
The recipe also carries `isla_surface_constant_gauge`, the centered frame with
a fixed length unit that was the program's configuration before the relative
frame. It is kept only to reproduce earlier measurements and to serve as the
diagnostic that shows what a sample-estimated center costs (its error grows
12x under a 10:1 sampling-density bias). Do not use it for new work.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Checkpoints remember their configuration"}
Every checkpoint stores its constructor arguments, so a model saved under a
variant loads in the configuration that trained it; you never have to
recall which frame a checkpoint used. A checkpoint that names one of the
research-only options removed from the class at its former
default loads unchanged; one that set such an option raises an error naming
the git tag `isla-research-full`, where the full research class remains
runnable with its tests.
:::

## What the model needs from your data {#sec-using-inputs}

The forward call is keyword-only, so the recipe's `forward_kwargs:` mapping
reads exactly as the call does. For the surface task:

```yaml
forward_kwargs:
  points: interior.points                                  # (B, N, 3) sampled cell centroids ("interior" is the datapipe's name for the sampled point set, not the fluid domain)
  normals: boundaries.vehicle.cell_data.normals            # (B, N, 3) unit outward normals
  measure_weights: interior.point_data._target_quadrature_measure   # (B, N) area each sampled cell stands for
  global_vectors: global_data.U_inf_dir                    # (B, 1, 3) the freestream as a unit direction
```

Three of these need a word.

- **The measure weights must sum to the surface area.** When the recipe
  keeps $n$ of $N$ cells, each kept cell carries the Horvitz–Thompson weight,
  its area times $N/n$, so that the total measure, which is ISLA's length
  unit, is the full surface area at any `sampling_resolution`. The surface
  dataset writes this as `_target_quadrature_measure`; the volume dataset
  writes the equivalent `quadrature_measure` through its
  `ComposeQuadratureMeasure` stage. Feeding raw sub-sampled areas shrinks the
  length unit by the kept fraction and moves every invariant out of its
  trained range.
- **The global vector must be a unit direction.** `ComputeFreestreamDirection`
  writes `U_inf_dir` from the physical velocity; the model normalizes it
  again internally and discards the magnitude. This is also the
  fair-comparison rule for every architecture in the book
  (@sec-fair-comparison): fed the physical velocity, GeoTransolver's global
  context collapses to one slice and loses 3.4 to 3.8x.
- **A speed or other magnitude that matters is a global scalar.** Set
  `n_global_scalars` and pass `global_scalars` of shape (B, S). No fixed power
  of the freestream speed is a physical law for every output (a pressure
  coefficient is degree zero, a dimensional pressure degree two), so the
  model learns the dependence like any other parameter.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Problems other than external aerodynamics"}
The architecture knows only that it was handed $K$ global directions and
$S$ global scalars. A buoyant flow passes gravity as its one direction; a
magnetized flow passes two; steady conduction with pinned temperatures
passes none (`n_global_vectors: 0`) and supplies the pinned values as
per-cell `boundary_scalars` (`n_boundary_scalars`). Each global direction
adds one seed cosine, one relational cosine and three vectors to the output
basis (@sec-mt2-inputs). The tests in `test_isla_global_inputs.py` cover
zero and two directions, global scalars, and the invariance of the output to
the magnitude of every global vector.
:::

## Training {#sec-using-train}

From the recipe root:

```bash
# DrivAerML surface, ISLA
python src/train.py model=isla_surface dataset=drivaer_ml_surface \
    training.optimizer.lr=1e-3 compile=false

# DrivAerML interior: boundary -> volume, queries as interacting tokens with the signed distance
python src/train.py model=isla_volume dataset=drivaer_ml_volume_reference \
    training.optimizer.lr=1e-3 compile=false

# HiLiftAeroML surface
python src/train.py model=isla_surface dataset=highlift_surface \
    training.optimizer.lr=1e-3 compile=false training.num_epochs=200 sampling_resolution=100000
```

The protocol behind every number in this book is 10,000 sampled cells per
case, 500 epochs, bfloat16 autocast, no augmentation, learning rate 1e-3 at
width 192, final-epoch checkpoint (@sec-protocol). ISLA needs no rotation
augmentation: the contracts make it exact, and a model trained in the
dataset's native frame predicts a car in any pose (@sec-pose).

### The width learning-rate rule {#sec-using-lr}

**Above width 192, set the learning rate to $10^{-3} \times 192 /
\mathrm{hidden}$.** At width 512 that is $3.75 \times 10^{-4}$. At the
protocol rate of $10^{-3}$ the relative frame diverges at width 512: the
routing hardens to one slice per token and the anchors collapse. Under the
rule it trains cleanly, and the rule costs a centered control at the same
corner nothing (its error at $3.75 \times 10^{-4}$ equals its error at
$10^{-3}$), so the rule is a property of the relative frame, not a
retuning of the comparison (@sec-nb-corner-wlr-verdict,
@sec-nb-cg-wlr-verdict). Within a decade of rate at width 192 ISLA is
stable where GeoTransolver degrades several-fold (@sec-robustness-lr).

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="The rule is provisional"}
The rule is adopted in the recipe config and documented here as the
program's working practice; it rests on one corner (width 512, 80,000
cells) and two controls. A width ladder at fixed cells would establish it as
a scaling law; until then treat it as the safe default rather than an
optimum.
:::

## Evaluation and the inference sampler {#sec-using-sampler}

Inference shares the training configuration and reads the checkpoint by
run identifier:

```bash
python src/infer.py model=isla_surface dataset=drivaer_ml_surface \
    run_id=<the trained run_id> infer_split=val sampling_resolution=10000 precision=float32
```

Report in float32. The recipe trains under bf16 autocast, and every number
in this book is a float32 inference on the final-epoch checkpoint
(@sec-metrics). A bf16 inference differs from the float32 one by about 2%
of the prediction from rounding alone, and under a rigid motion of the
input its prediction moves by about 4% (pressure) and 7% (wall shear),
where the float32 prediction moves by 3e-5 (@sec-mt2-contracts). Where the
pose or the sampling-consistency contract is load-bearing, infer in
float32.

**For inference at a fixed cell budget, draw the cells with the stratified
sampler.** Replace the dataset's `SubsampleMesh` stage with the recipe's
`StratifiedSubsampleMesh`:

```yaml
    - _target_: ${dp:StratifiedSubsampleMesh}   # was SubsampleMesh
      n_cells: ${sampling_resolution}
```

It keeps the same inclusion law (every cell kept with probability $n/N$,
weight $N/n$), so nothing about the trained model or the quantity it
estimates changes, but the kept cells are a *systematic* draw along the
Morton order of the cell centroids, one per consecutive run of $N/n$ cells
with a single random offset. A systematic sample has the same expectation as
an independent draw for every cell-weighted integral and a lower variance
for smooth integrands. The effect is a free improvement for every model and
largest for ISLA, whose slice states are the noisiest estimates
(@sec-deficit-anatomy):

```{python}
#| label: tbl-using-strat
#| output: asis
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
qv = json.load(open(RES / "quadvar_reduction_2026-09-17.json"))["arms"]
mean = statistics.mean
names = [("isla_ref", "ISLA"), ("gt_unit", "GeoTransolver"), ("transolver_unit", "Transolver")]
out = "| model | independent draw | stratified draw | change |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|\n"
for k, lab in names:
    a = qv[k]; u = a["unif"]["10000"]; ind = mean(u["seeds"]) if isinstance(u, dict) else u
    st = mean(a["strat"]["10000"]["seeds"])
    out += f"| {lab} | {ind:.4f} | {st:.4f} | {(st/ind-1)*100:+.1f}% |\n"
print(out)
print(": DrivAerML surface pressure (area-weighted relative L2, float32, 48 validation cars, 10,000 cells, seed means) "
      "for the same checkpoints under the independent and the stratified inference draw. How to read this: the change is "
      "an evaluation effect on fixed checkpoints; it does not alter the ranking of the models, only the size of the gap. "
      "Data: results/quadvar_reduction_2026-09-17.json. {#tbl-using-strat}")
```

The book keeps the independent draw for its headline comparisons and
reports the stratified draw as a labeled row (@sec-scoreboard); for a
deployment, use the stratified draw, or more cells.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="How many cells"}
The in-distribution gap to the baselines halves from the 10,000-cell
independent draw to 80,000 cells, because most of it is estimator variance
in the slice states (@sec-deficit-anatomy). The default compiled step is
2.2x GeoTransolver's at 40,000 tokens; the fused geometry kernel
(`+model.geo_kernel=fused`, CUDA only, exact) brings it to parity there
(@sec-using-cost). If the budget allows 40,000 cells, use them with the fused
kernel; if it allows 10,000, use the stratified draw.
:::

## Loading a trained model {#sec-using-checkpoint}

A saved ISLA is a PhysicsNeMo module checkpoint and loads with the class's
`from_checkpoint`; the constructor arguments are stored inside it, so no
configuration has to be repeated. A checkpoint written under the class's
former name loads through the compatibility alias. The forward call in your
own code mirrors the recipe mapping:

```python
from physicsnemo.experimental.nn import ISLA
model = ISLA.from_checkpoint("checkpoints/isla_surface.mdlus").eval()
out = model(points=x, normals=n, measure_weights=w, global_vectors=g_hat)  # (B, N, 1 + 3)
p, tau = out[..., :1], out[..., 1:]
```

`points` and `normals` are (B, N, 3), `measure_weights` (B, N) summing to the
surface area, `global_vectors` (B, 1, 3) or (B, 3) for one direction. The
output stacks the scalar fields first, then each vector field's three
components. For interior prediction with `isla_volume`, add `query_points`,
`query_normals` (the signed-distance gradient) and `query_scalars` (the signed
distance) and read the output at the query rows; deploy at the training query
count of 10,000, because the interacting decode's prediction at a point
depends on the joint query set (@sec-interior-companion).

## Cost {#sec-using-cost}

At the recipe dimensions ISLA has 8.9M parameters (GeoTransolver 9.0M). On
one GB300 in bfloat16, batch of one case, both models compiled as the
recipe runs them, the training step at 10,000 tokens is 47 ms at 1.30 GiB
with the geometry recompute on, against GeoTransolver's 45 ms at 2.70 GiB;
switching the recompute off gives 39 ms at 1.94 GiB. At 40,000 tokens the
default path is 119 ms against 53 ms and the fused kernel 52 ms at 4.5
against 10.0 GiB (@tbl-mt2-cost). Two practical consequences:

- **Leave `geo_checkpoint: true` unless you are short of time and long on
  memory.** It is bitwise identical in outputs and gradients.
- **Use `+model.geo_kernel=fused` at 40,000 tokens and above.** It computes
  the same function (relative difference at most $5.5 \times 10^{-7}$ in
  bf16) and is opt-in only because it requires CUDA and Triton.

The passive decoder adds 1.1M parameters and four read blocks; the
query-token interior configuration adds almost no parameters but spans every
token with the per-slice geometry, at 0.28 s per step and 6.0 GB at 10,000
interior queries.

## Contracts you can check on your own data {#sec-using-contracts}

The contracts are exact properties of the code (@sec-mt2-contracts), and
each is cheap to verify on a loaded checkpoint: rotate and translate the
inputs by a random rigid motion and compare the scalars (unchanged) and the
vectors (rotated); scale the points by $k$ and the measure weights by $k^2$
(unchanged). In float32 the residuals are of order $10^{-5}$ on the
trained checkpoints; in bf16 autocast several percent, mostly rounding. A residual far above these on your own data means
the inputs, not the model: normals with inconsistent orientation, weights
that do not sum to the surface area, or positions that were already centered
or scaled by something sample-dependent before the model saw them. (The
model normalizes the normals and the global vectors itself, so their
magnitudes cannot cause a residual.)
